evidence.title: OOD Detectors Are Best Used Runtime Verifiers, Not Semantic Shift Classifiers
evidence.outcome: Expected lifetime cost per patient with OOD runtime verifiers versus conventional system in polyp segmentation
evidence.effect: Implementing OOD detectors as runtime verifiers reduced expected costs per patient by upwards of 40% versus a conventionally implemented system.
evidence.quote: Our results show that implementing OOD detectors as runtime verifiers reduces the expected costs per patient by upwards of 40%.

evidence.title: SIGNAL: A Scalable, Real-World Model for Rapid Intraoperative Molecular Classification of Gliomas Using Stimulated Raman Histology
evidence.outcome: Attention-based rejection of uninformative images (blood, acellular regions) before classification, versus model without rejection
evidence.effect: DeepGlioma without image rejection underperformed on uncurated data (72.59% accuracy); SIGNAL with attention filtering reached 90.10%. Attention correlated with cellularity (r=0.96) and negatively with blood coverage (r=-0.99).
evidence.quote: SIGNAL’s attention mechanism had a strong positive linear correlation with mean patch cellularity (r=0.96, p<0.001) and a strong negative correlation with patch blood coverage (r=-0.99,p<0.001).

evidence.title: DeepFundus: A flow-cytometry-like image quality classifier for boosting the whole life cycle of medical artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic AI sensitivity/accuracy for drusen in good vs poor quality images after DeepFundus filtering
evidence.effect: Overall quality filter: drusen sensitivity 0.853 (GQ) vs 0.494 (PQ), difference 0.360, p<0.001; accuracy 0.938 vs 0.914, p=0.002. Similar results in other 6 filters.
evidence.quote: the GQ group demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity and accuracy values.

evidence.title: Quantifying Epistemic Uncertainty in Predictions for Safer Health AI Performance Under Dataset Shifts

evidence.title: InfoOOD: information bottleneck optimization for post hoc medical image out-of-distribution detection
evidence.outcome: OOD detection AUC for simulated CT artifacts, InfoOOD vs established OOD detectors
evidence.effect: InfoOOD AUC 0.93 vs 0.57 for embedded feature-based measures (strong rings artifact); AUC 0.75 vs 0.61 for reconstruction-based measure (weak sparse view artifact).
evidence.quote: TheInfoOODmeasure consistently outperformed the embedded feature-based measures in detecting OOD data (e.g. AUC = 0.93 vs. AUC = 0.57 for the strong rings artifact) and surpassed the reconstruction-based measure across weak magnitude artifacts (e.g., AUC = 0.75 vs. AUC = 0.61 for the weak sparse view artifact).

evidence.title: Complete Blood Count and Monocyte Distribution Width-Based Machine Learning Algorithms for Sepsis Detection: Multicentric Development and External Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Performance when a key input (MDW) was entirely missing, using imputation
evidence.effect: Lack of MDW (100% missing) led to a large decrease in PPV despite imputation, though overall performance was acceptable.
evidence.quote: While, indeed, the obtained results show that acceptable results could be obtained even in the presence of significant missingness shift, the lack of MDW led to a relevant drop in performance, thus highlighting the need for collecting complete data in practical scenarios.

commentary.bottom_line: Sixteen studies tested input detectors, and all reported that flagging missing, low-quality, or out-of-distribution inputs improved detection of unreliable outputs or downstream model accuracy, but every test ran offline, in simulation, or on benchmarks. No study measured whether detectors change clinical decisions or patient outcomes in live care.

perspectives.view: All 16 tests are level 4 or 5 designs run offline or on benchmarks. They measure detector AUROC or downstream accuracy rather than patient outcomes. Results point in one direction, though one study found benefit inconsistent across detectors and age subgroups. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and risk of bias.

In a Belgian failure-mode analysis, a case-specific report flagging out-of-training-distribution inputs lowered the lack-of-detectability score for bad predictions from 8.17 to 3.51. About 3% residual risk remained that staff overlook the report. Correct predictions appeared in all reliability categories in one external validation, so flags may also withhold usable outputs.

On uncurated glioma images, rejecting uninformative regions raised accuracy from 72.59% to 90.10%. Fundus quality filtering separated drusen sensitivity of 0.853 in good images from 0.494 in poor images. These studies suggest filters may work on real image streams, but none measured clinician response to flags or workflow burden in deployment.

No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. In a safety-net, rural deployment in India, an AI gradability check had 8% specificity and labeled 21 (42%) human-ungradable cataract eyes as gradable. This hazard study suggests detectors may fail where image quality is poorest.

One Mahalanobis-distance detector ran in seconds on a CPU with 92% AUROC for failed segmentations, which suggests low computing cost. A simulation estimated that runtime verifiers cut expected per-patient cost by upwards of 40% in polyp segmentation. No study reported staffing or review time needed to handle flagged cases.

Hazard studies show that missing inputs degraded performance across 20,334 silently deployed laboratory models and that 8 of 1,570 CTA cases produced errors from poor-quality images. No test examined whether patients learn that an input was flagged or whether a flag sends their case to a clinician.

commentary.research_gap: No study deployed an input detector in live care with a comparison group, so its effect on clinician decisions, missed diagnoses, and patient harm is unknown. Prospective or stepped-wedge studies should measure flag rates, clinician handling of flagged cases, false-flag burden, and patient outcomes, including in settings with frequent missing data or poor image quality.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the 16 tests included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net data come from a hazard study in rural India, where an AI gradability check classified 42% of human-ungradable cataract eyes as gradable. Health systems serving these groups should not assume that benchmark detector performance will transfer to their patients.
